description.summary: A king of the demons in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions, best known as the antagonist of the Book of Tobit, as a builder-figure in Talmudic legends of King Solomon, and as the goetic king Asmoday of the Lesser Key of Solomon.
description.full: Asmodeus (Hebrew Ashmedai; Greek Asmodaios; Arabic Sakhr) is a major demon figure in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic demonology. His name probably derives from the Avestan compound aēšma-daēva, 'wrath-demon', suggesting a Zoroastrian origin or influence. He first appears in the deuterocanonical Book of Tobit (c. 2nd century BCE), where he kills the seven successive husbands of Sarah on their wedding nights and is finally driven off and bound in Egypt by the angel Raphael. In Talmudic literature he is the king of the shedim and a more mischievous figure, famously tricked by Solomon into helping build the Temple in Jerusalem before stealing Solomon's throne. Christian demonology of the late medieval and early modern period assigned him oversight of the deadly sin of lust (Peter Binsfeld; Malleus Maleficarum, 1486) and integrated him as a great king or duke into grimoiric demonology — most famously as Asmoday, king number 32 in the Ars Goetia of the Lesser Key of Solomon, ruling 72 legions, depicted with three heads (bull, man, ram), a serpent's tail, and a fire-breathing mouth, riding an infernal dragon. In Islamic tradition he appears as Sakhr ('rock'), the demon imprisoned in stone after his defeat by Solomon, central to Quranic exegesis of Sūrat Ṣād 38:34 and to the Tale of the City of Brass.

etymology.origin: Most widely accepted derivation: Avestan aēšma-daēva, 'demon of wrath', though the compound is not directly attested in surviving Avestan scripture. The Hebrew Ashmedai and Greek Asmodaios derive from this stem.
etymology.meaning: 'Demon of wrath' (Avestan); rendered in later Christian demonology as the demon of lust.
etymology.first_use: Book of Tobit (deuterocanonical Jewish text, c. 225–175 BCE).

taxonomy.variant: Goetic king (Ars Goetia no. 32) / Talmudic king of shedim

features.description: Per the Ars Goetia: 'three heads, the first like a bull, the second like a man, the third like a ram'
Flames issue from his mouth (Ars Goetia)
In the Ars Goetia he is shown mounted on an infernal dragon, holding a lance and banner

Collin de Plancy's 1818 Dictionnaire Infernal depicts him with a man's chest, a rooster's leg, a serpent's tail, three heads (man breathing fire, sheep, bull), riding a fire-breathing lion with dragon wings

physical.morphology: Iconographically composite: anthropomorphic torso with multiple heads, mounted on a beast, with serpentine and avian elements. Earlier (Tobit, Talmud) descriptions are non-iconic.

abilities.description: In Tobit, kills Sarah's seven successive husbands on their wedding nights
Per the Ars Goetia, Asmoday governs 72 legions of inferior spirits

abilities.ability: Mathematics, geometry, and the mechanical arts
abilities.description: Ars Goetia: he 'teacheth the arts of arithmetic, astronomy, geometry, and all handicrafts'
Ars Goetia attributes the location of buried treasures to him
Ars Goetia: gives 'the ring of virtues'
In late medieval and early modern Christian demonology, presides over lust and gaming-house vice (Binsfeld; Malleus Maleficarum, 1486)
Talmudic: forced by Solomon to gather the shamir worm and labour on the Temple

habitat_preference: deserted places (after his binding in Egypt per Tobit)
patterns: Targets marriages and disrupts the consummation of unions (Tobit)
Engages with Solomon as both adversary and instrument of construction
Listed as one of the seven 'princes of Hell' overseeing the deadly sin of lust

range.description: A textual phenomenon distributed across the literatures of the Abrahamic world: the Hebrew Bible deuterocanon, Talmud and midrash, Christian demonology, Islamic Quranic commentary and the Arabian Nights, and Western occult grimoires. Veneration / invocation occurs only in marginal occult or magical contexts.
regions: Christian Europe (medieval and early-modern grimoiric tradition)

peak_activity_periods.description: Jewish demonological tradition (Tobit, Testament of Solomon, Talmud)
Christian demonological codification (Malleus Maleficarum 1486; Pseudomonarchia Daemonum 1577; Lesser Key of Solomon 17th c.)
Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire Infernal popularises modern iconographic Asmodeus

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Demonologists (Binsfeld) assigned him peak power in November; the zodiacal sign of Aquarius (Jan 30 – Feb 8).

origins.cultural_roots: Probable Zoroastrian/Iranian origin (Aēšma) absorbed into Second Temple Jewish demonology. From there into Christian and Islamic traditions.
origins.earliest_accounts: The Book of Tobit (deuterocanonical, composed c. 225–175 BCE). The Testament of Solomon (1st–3rd c. CE) and the Babylonian Talmud (Gittin 68a–b) develop the figure.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to Lilith, Samael, the goetic kings, and the Islamic Sakhr; absorbed into the wider 'demon king' / 'lord of hell' tradition.

timeline.event: Book of Tobit composed; Asmodeus appears as the slayer of Sarah's bridegrooms, bound by Raphael in Egypt
Testament of Solomon develops the Asmodeus-Solomon legend
Babylonian Talmud, tractate Gittin (68a–68b), develops the story of Solomon, Ashmedai, and the shamir worm
Heinrich Kramer publishes the Malleus Maleficarum, naming Asmodeus the demon of lust
timeline.significance: Codifies his role in Christian demonology of the witch-trial era

timeline.event: Johann Weyer publishes Pseudomonarchia Daemonum, listing Asmodeus as 'Sidonay', a king ruling 72 legions
Luis Vélez de Guevara publishes El diablo cojuelo, reimagining Asmodeus as a witty mischievous spirit
Alain-René Lesage publishes Le Diable boiteux, popularising the genial 'limping devil' Asmodeus
Jacques Collin de Plancy publishes Dictionnaire Infernal, with Louis Le Breton's classic engraved Asmodeus

history.modern_era: Asmodeus has remained one of the most iconic of the demonic kings in popular culture, fantasy gaming (especially Dungeons & Dragons, where he is archdevil of the Nine Hells), occult fiction, and horror cinema. The Lesser Key of Solomon has been continuously reprinted in modern occult publishing since S. L. MacGregor Mathers and Aleister Crowley's 1904 edition.

documentary.name: Book of Tobit
documentary.description: Deuterocanonical Jewish text in which Asmodeus appears as the principal antagonist, killing Sarah's seven husbands and being driven off and bound by the angel Raphael.
documentary.analysis: Foundational text for the Asmodeus tradition.

documentary.name: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 68a–b
documentary.description: Canonical Talmudic narrative of Solomon, Ashmedai, the shamir worm, and Ashmedai's usurpation of Solomon's throne.
documentary.analysis: Central Jewish development of the Asmodeus tradition.
documentary.source: Babylonian Talmud, Soncino edition and others

documentary.name: Ars Goetia (Lesser Key of Solomon), no. 32
documentary.description: Lists Asmoday as king of demons no. 32, with three heads, dragon mount, governing 72 legions, and teaching arithmetic, astronomy, geometry, and crafts.
documentary.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers / A. Crowley, The Goetia (1904)

paranormal.name: Demonic prince / king of Hell
paranormal.description: Mainstream demonological view in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions: Asmodeus is a real spiritual entity, a fallen angel or demon-king, who can be invoked or warded against by ritual.
proponents: Authors of the Book of Tobit
Compilers of the Lesser Key of Solomon

scientific.name: Iranian / Zoroastrian etymological origin
scientific.description: Comparative-religion view: Asmodeus is a Hellenistic-period adoption of the Avestan demon of wrath Aēšma-daēva, whose attributes were progressively reshaped within Jewish and Christian demonology.
evidence_cited: Etymological correspondence Avestan aēšma-daēva → Hebrew Ashmedai

scientific.name: Literary and narrative figure
scientific.description: Standard scholarly view: Asmodeus is a literary character of Second Temple Jewish, rabbinic, Christian, and Islamic textual traditions, whose iconography crystallises in the early modern grimoiric tradition.
evidence_cited: Textual genealogy of the figure across Tobit, Talmud, Testament of Solomon, Ars Goetia, Dictionnaire Infernal

skeptical.name: Pre-scientific personification of human passions
skeptical.description: Skeptical view: Asmodeus and the goetic kings personify human vices (wrath, lust, greed) and were used to externalise moral failure in ritual and pastoral contexts.
evidence_cited: Functional alignment of Asmodeus with the deadly sin of lust
Use of demonological treatises as moral-pastoral instruments

traditions: Tobit-cycle Christian and Jewish liturgical readings
Talmudic narrative of Solomon and Ashmedai
Islamic story of Sakhr in the Tale of the City of Brass (1001 Nights)
Western ceremonial-magic tradition invoking the Goetic kings
stories: Tobias, the fish, and the binding of Asmodeus in Egypt (Tobit 6–8)
Solomon, the shamir worm, and the building of the Temple (Gittin 68a–b)
The Tale of the City of Brass (1001 Nights)
folklore.beliefs: Asmodeus stands in Western demonological tradition as one of the canonical kings or princes of Hell, often paired with the deadly sin of lust.
